slides.title: Motivation: The Problem with In-Order Issue
slides.text:
Motivation: The Problem with In-Order Issue
In-order issue: issue follows program order; an unready head blocks everything behind it.
(a ready instruction cannot pass an unready predecessor — a direct limit on performance)
I1: fld    f0, 0(x1)     # cache miss, long latency
I2: fadd.d f4, f4, f0    # RAW — must wait for I1
I3: fadd.d f6, f8, f10   # fully independent of I1/I2
• I1 — cache miss, long-latency wait
• I2 — RAW through f0, waits for I1
• I3 — operands ready, ALU free, yet blocked behind
• Head-of-line blocking — ready elements cannot pass an 
unready queue head
• Multiple issue allows together, never passing; in-order 
superscalar shares the limit
→ We need out-of-order (OoO) execution or called dynamic (run-time) scheduling.
Btw, why use FP instructions? Integer ALU operations 
take one cycle, so an unready head costs little.
fld: Floating-point Load Doubleword
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 2. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

slides.title: Dynamic Scheduling: Scoreboarding → Tomasulo
slides.text:
Dynamic Scheduling: Scoreboarding → Tomasulo
CDC 6600 (delivered from 1964); the scoreboard was 
this machine’s central control mechanism. Photo: Jitze 
Couperus, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
For scientific computing (FP, Multiply)
Historical note
The idea of OoO execution predated VLSI 
density (1978, DARPA, VLSI project) and 
classic 5-stage pipelining (1980s), and 
cache (1968):  mainframe-only for decades, 
mainstream once transistor budgets 
allowed it
1964
CDC 6600 · Scoreboarding
· central status tables
· out-of-order execution / write result
· no renaming → WAR / WAW stalls remain
1967
IBM System/360 Model 91 · Tomasulo
· distributed reservation stations
· tag renaming at issue
· the common data bus (CDB) broadcast
+ WAR / WAW removed
Ball back: 1964 was a landmark year for computer architecture: 
alongside the CDC 6600, IBM announced System/360 (chief architect 
Gene Amdahl), defining the compatible-family ISA paradigm.
discrete component 分立原件
integrated circuits 集成电路

slides.title: Hardware Background of CDC 6600
slides.text:
Hardware background of CDC6600
 Global lockstep pipeline (MIPS 5-stage)
1980s
CDC 6600 (scoreboard, independent FUs)
1964
Clock One global clock; all pipeline registers update together Shared clock, but no single chained pipeline; each FU runs 
independently
Progress All instructions advance in lockstep; a stall freezes the 
whole pipeline
Each FU advances on its own; one blocked FU blocks no other
Structure Fixed chain of stages: IF–ID–EX–MEM–WB Parallel independent functional units — not a series pipe
Model Hardware pipeline registers Per-instruction state machine (Issue / Read / Execute / Write Result)
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 4. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

slides.title: Refresh: The Five Pipeline Stages in Hardware
slides.text:
Refresh: The Five Pipeline Stages in Hardware
IF/ID ID/EX EX/MEM MEM/WB
IF
Fetch ID
Decode EX
Execute MEM
Memory WB
Write back
IF — Fetch
Read the instruction at 
PC from the instruction 
memory; an adder 
forms PC + 4.
Hardware: PC register, 
I-memory, adder
ID — Decode
Decode the opcode 
into control signals; 
read rs / rt from the 
register file; 
sign-extend the 
immediate.
Hardware: Control 
unit, register-file read 
ports, sign extender
EX — Execute
The ALU computes the 
result, the load / store 
address, or the branch 
condition and target.
Hardware: ALU, 
branch adder
MEM — Memory
A load reads, a store 
writes data memory at 
the EX address; other 
instructions pass 
through.
Hardware: D-memory 
read / write ports
WB — Write back
A multiplexer selects 
the ALU result or the 
loaded data and writes 
it to the destination 
register.
Hardware: 
Register-file write port, 
MUX
Pipeline registers (IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM, MEM/WB) latch every signal at each clock edge — the “lockstep” the 
previous slide contrasts with the CDC 6600.
Diagram redrawn after the classic RISC pipeline figure — Patterson & Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design, ch. 4; 
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_RISC_pipeline

slides.title: Scoreboarding: Issue Stage
slides.text:
What the Issue stage does (CDC 6600 scoreboard model):
1. Check: a functional unit is free; no WAW conflict with an in-flight instruction
2. Allocate a free functional unit
3. Add a row in the Instruction Status table, state = Issue
4. In the Unit Status table: FU.Busy = Yes; record Op, Fi (destination), Fj / Fk (sources)
5. Register Result Status table: RegisterResult[Fi] = this FU
In essence, issue dispatches the instruction to an FU and registers it in the central 
scoreboard, and the instruction then waits to read operands and execute. It moves from the 
fetch queue to the FU / scoreboard — nothing is written to the architectural register file 
yet.
Scoreboarding: Issue Stage
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 6. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

slides.title: Scoreboarding: Overview
slides.text:
Scoreboarding: Overview
Scoreboarding is a scheduling algorithm. The scoreboard: Maintain one central hardware table (3 subtables), 
answering each cycle — can it issue? are operands ready? can the result be written? It has 4 stages (not 
corresponding to 4 stages in pipelining).
Stage Action Stall when
1. Issue allocate a free unit structural (no free unit) · WAW in-flight writer
(because of no renaming)
2. Read operands read valid sources RAW — a source is in flight
3. Execute compute; may reorder —
4. Write result write via result bus, forward WAR — an earlier reader needs the old value
(because of no renaming)
Three tables
● Instruction status
● Functional unit (FU) status
● register result status
Achieved
In-order issue · OoO execution 
and write result; RAW via waiting 
+ bus forwarding
Not achieved
Register names persist: WAW 
blocks issue, WAR blocks 
writeback
Scoreboarding routes around RAW waits at run time; name dependences still block issue and 
writeback —> Tomasulo algorithm (1967).
I1: fadd f4, f0, f1
I2: fmul f4, f8, f10
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 7. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

slides.title: Scoreboarding — Animated Walkthrough
slides.text:
⭐
 Scoreboarding — Animated Walkthrough
The program, line by line
LD F6, 34(R2): F6 = Mem[R2 + 34] — base register 
R2 + displacement 34 (bytes).
LD F2, 45(R3): F2 = Mem[R3 + 45].
MULTD F0, F2, F4: F0 = F2 × F4 — the pattern is OP 
Fi, Fj, Fk, i.e. Fi = Fj op Fk.
F0–F10 are floating-point registers; R2/R3 are 
integer (address) registers.
Reading the tables: Fi = destination register; 
Fj/Fk = sources; Qj/Qk = the unit that will produce 
that operand (who to wait for); Rj/Rk = operand 
value ready and not yet read.
Watch I6 (ADDD): blocked at issue (Add busy — 
structural), then finished at cycle 12 but cannot 
write F6 until DIVD reads it (WAR, cycle 18).
Completion order 1, 2, 4, 3, 6, 5 — out-of-order, 
yet the final register file matches in-order 
execution.
How to read: every number is a clock cycle, counted from cycle 1 (top right of the frame). Gold cells mark exactly what changed this cycle — follow 
the gold to find each cycle's event. A value written at cycle c can be read at cycle c + 1.
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 8. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026. The supplied PDF contains a static snapshot; its original animation is not included.

slides.title: From Scoreboarding to Tomasulo
slides.text:
So far:  in-order issue has head-of-line blocking; scoreboarding executes out of order but still 
stalls on WAR and WAW name dependences.
Next:  build the four components — reservation stations, renaming at issue, the common data 
bus, wakeup — then derive four instructions on the board.
Why it matters:  these four components are the direct ancestors of the scheduler in every 
modern out-of-order core, including gem5’s O3CPU in Lab 7.
Next: Tomasulo’s Algorithm
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 9. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

slides.title: Tomasulo: The Man, Two Principles, Two Terms
slides.text:
Tomasulo: The Man, Two Principles, Two Terms
1967
Robert M. Tomasulo, IBM Computer Scientist, System/360 Model 91
The flagship scientific machine of the System/360 family; its floating-point unit ran the 
algorithm — built from discrete logic, no compiler involved.  
Paper: An Efficient Algorithm for Exploiting Multiple Arithmetic Units (IBM J. R&D, 1967) [URL]
P1 — Hardware decides readiness
Not the compiler: an instruction executes when its 
operands are ready and its functional unit is free — 
not when its turn in program order comes
P2 — Register renaming
At issue, register names are replaced by fresh tags; 
WAR and WAW name dependences disappear, RAW 
survives as a tag chain
Term — Reservation station (RS)
A small waiting queue in front of each unit; every entry 
holds one issued instruction: the operation and each 
operand as a value or a tag
Term — Common data bus (CDB)
One broadcast channel: each finished result (tag + 
value) reaches every waiting station and the register 
file in the same cycle
1997 Eckert–Mauchly Award
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 10. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

slides.title: Reservation Stations: Value or Provenance
slides.text:
⭐
 Reservation Stations: Value or Provenance
One entry = all hardware state of one issued, unfinished instruction:
Field Holds Valid when
busy entry occupied? set at issue, cleared after write result
Op operation (fadd / fmul...) selects the unit class
Vj, Vk source values already available; copied at issue
Qj, Qk producer tags pending → non-empty; CDB match 
clears Q into V
A effective address load/store buffers only; once base is 
ready
Qi[f] — register result status
One tag per architectural register, 
pointing to the station that will write f; 
empty = stored value valid
Each operand slot: exactly one of 
value/tag
Add1: fadd · Qj=L1 · Vk=f0 · busy=1
Snapshot at issue
Operands are fixed from then on; later 
register rewrites cannot affect a waiting 
station
Each source operand answers one question: is the value already here (in V), or must a tag be 
waited for (in Q)? The instruction no longer remembers its original register names.
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 11. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

slides.title: Renaming at Issue: Names Become Fresh Tags
slides.text:
⭐
 Renaming at Issue: Names Become Fresh Tags
The four-instruction board example: tag assignment at issue, cycle by cycle:
Cycle Instruction Station taken: operands recorded as Qi after issue
c1 I1: fld f2,0(x1) L1: A=0(x1) Qi[f2]=L1
c2 I2: fadd.d f4,f2,f0 Add1: Qj=L1, Vk=f0 Qi[f4]=A1
c3 I3: fmul.d f6,f8,f10 Mul1: Vj=f8(old), Vk=f10 Qi[f6]=M1
c4 I4: fadd.d f8,f4,f6 Add2: Qj=A1, Qk=M1 Qi[f8]=A2
WAR removed
I3 reads f8, I4 writes it: the old value 
is in Vj at c3; I4 gets fresh A2 and 
need not wait
WAW removed
Same-name writers get distinct 
tags; Qi always points to the latest; 
no coupling through the name
RAW retained
True deps become tag chains: 
I2←L1, I4←A1/M1; produced values 
arrive via the CDB
Hardware register renaming: at issue, architectural names map to physical result locations named 
by tags. Name dependences arise from sharing one name; an exclusive name per in-flight 
instruction removes them.
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 12. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

slides.title: The Common Data Bus: One Broadcast, All Compare
slides.text:
⭐
 The Common Data Bus: One Broadcast, All Compare
(1) Broadcast
The finisher drives (its tag, the result); one per cycle, others 
arbitrate
(2) Wakeup
All stations compare Qj/Qk in parallel; match → value into V, Q 
cleared — comparator hardware, not a lookup
(3) Select
Both Q empty and the unit free → candidate; arbitration picks who 
runs this cycle
(4) Register file, same cycle
Matching Qi → write value, clear tag; bus forwarding — no 
write-then-read wait
The CDB generalizes L3 forwarding: L3 bypassed one result to the next instruction’s execute stage; 
the CDB broadcasts a result to all waiters and the register file at once.
L1 finishes
CDB: broadcast (L1, mem[f2])
Add1
Qj=L1 ✓ woken
Add2
Qj=A1: no match
Mul1
V ready: unaffected
Register file: Qi[f2]=L1 ✓
write f2, clear the tag
Select: Add1 ready, adder free → runs next cycle
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 13. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

slides.title: The Three Phases
slides.text:
⭐
 The Three Phases
1
Issue — rename, park
Take the head; require a free 
station
Valid source → V; otherwise 
Q=Qi[src]
Qi[dst] ← this tag
Stall: no free entry (structural) — 
issue freezes
2
Execute — wait, compute
Both Q empty (or address A ready) 
→ the unit computes
Before that, the instruction merely 
waits
RAW — await the producer’s CDB 
broadcast; execution goes out of 
order
3
Write result — broadcast, 
free
Drive (tag, result) onto the CDB
Matching Q → copy value, clear Q; 
matching Qi → write register, clear 
tag
Free the station
Wait: CDB busy → arbitration, one 
per cycle
Terms:  classic “issue” = enter station and rename, usually 
“dispatch” today; modern “issue” means wakeup/select out 
of the station (see the glossary)
No software involved:  per-cycle decisions are comparator 
and arbitration circuits; the compiler only supplies the ISA 
program
The three constraint classes are each handled: structural hazards block at issue, RAW waits before 
execute, and WAR/WAW simply do not exist after renaming at issue.
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 14. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

slides.title: Tomasulo’s Algorithm — Animated Walkthrough
slides.text:
⭐
 Tomasulo's Algorithm — Animated Walkthrough
Same six instructions as the 
scoreboard animation — watch 
what is missing: no structural issue 
stalls, no WAR write stall.
Reservation stations hold each 
operand as a value (V) or a producer 
tag (Q); the register status Qi says 
who will write each register.
CDB broadcast: a finished result 
(tag + value) fills every matching Q 
in the same cycle — tags become 
values (wakeup).
Why no WAR stall: DIVD's source 
was renamed to a station tag at 
issue; ADDD writes the architectural 
F6 without harming anyone.
Example: Hennessy & Patterson, Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach — animation created for this course.
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 15. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026. The supplied PDF contains a static snapshot; its original animation is not included.

slides.title: Summary: Scoreboarding vs. Tomasulo
slides.text:
Summary: Scoreboarding vs. Tomasulo
Aspect Scoreboard (CDC 6600, 1964) Tomasulo (IBM 360/91, 1967)
Where status lives One central scoreboard (three tables) Distributed — in the reservation stations and the Qi 
register tags
Dependence tracking Watches register names; polls operand 
readiness each cycle
Tags (Qi) track producers; the CDB pushes results by 
broadcast
Name dependences 
WAR/WAW
Not eliminated — WAW stalls issue, WAR stalls 
writeback
Eliminated — names are decoupled by renaming at 
issue
Result delivery Wait for the register-file writeback, then read 
the register
CDB bypass broadcast — waiters receive the value in 
the broadcast cycle
Same goal — dynamic scheduling at run time. The difference is distribution + renaming + 
broadcast: the scoreboard’s questions answered without a central table, without 
name-dependence stalls, and without waiting for writeback.
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 16. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

slides.title: Onwards: From 1967 to Today
slides.text:
Onwards: From 1967 to Today
Historical lesson: ideas predate technology
1967: comparators and buffers too costly → mainframe-only for 
decades; 1990s: on-chip budgets allow it → standard in 
general-purpose cores
1995: three lines converge; the structure 
persists
μops (L6) + Tomasulo (L7) + ROB·prediction·speculation (L8) — 
this lecture builds the middle block
Equivalents in modern cores
reservation stations → issue queue (scheduler);  tags → 
physical-register numbers;  register status table → register 
alias table
names change; the “value or provenance” wait logic does not
In-order cores did not disappear
Energy-first embedded and “little” cores still issue in order; 
microarchitecture is a cost–benefit choice, not a replacement
1967
Tomasulo’s algorithm
mainframe era: hardware costly
1995
three lines converge
μops + Tomasulo + ROB/speculation
2000s–now
Issue queue + physical register file
tags are register numbers; ROBs: hundreds
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 17. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

slides.title: Summary: What Out-of-Order Buys and What It Costs
slides.text:
Summary: What Out-of-Order Buys and What It Costs
Gains
● tolerates latencies known only at run time (misses, 
bus occupancy, long ops)
● fills issue slots: one chain waits, independent chains 
use the units
● binary portability: wider windows in new cores, no 
recompilation
Costs
area and power: 
● stations and comparators run in parallel every 
cycle; 
● wakeup logic is on the frequency critical path 
design and verification complexity; 
● speculation adds a microarchitectural side-channel 
surface (L8)
Measured magnitudes (typical general-purpose 
cores)
0.5–1   in-order cores
2–4   wide OoO cores · typical general code
6–8   peaks on ILP-rich regular code
Far below the issue-width peak: short blocks, RAW chains, 
misses and branches cap it; returns diminish with window size 
(Wall 1993; quantified in L8)
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 18. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

slides.title: History: A Detour to Out-of-Order Execution
slides.text:
History: A Detour to Out-of-Order Execution
1964
CDC 6600 · 
scoreboard
First dynamic 
scheduling (S. Cray): ten 
heterogeneous 
functional units, 
out-of-order 
completion.
FP latencies differ by up 
to 40× — no fixed 
schedule can fit.
1967
IBM 360/91 · 
Tomasulo
Renaming tags + CDB 
broadcast: WAR/WAW 
eliminated by 
construction.
CAM compare and the 
broadcast bus are 
costly in discrete 
transistors — dynamic 
scheduling goes 
dormant.
1980s
RISC · five-stage 
pipeline
ISA co-designed with 
the pipeline: fixed 
format, load/store, 
single-cycle ALU.
In-order lockstep wins 
on clock rate and 
compiler-friendliness; 
out-of-order is shelved.
1990s
OoO returns · 
Tomasulo + ROB
Clock-rate wall: ILP 
becomes the only way 
forward.
Renaming + in-order 
commit via the reorder 
buffer — Pentium Pro 
(1995) makes 
out-of-order 
mainstream.
Today
Both live on
Five-stage pipeline: the 
teaching baseline and 
the embedded core.
OoO superscalar: every 
high-performance core 
— the 1964 idea, 
mainstream at last.
Lessons:
● Technologies come and go, but insights are forever.
● 技术的成败会随着条件变化 The success or failure of a tech is up to its condition.
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 19. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

slides.title: Three Gaps Remain — All Closed in L8
slides.text:
⭐
 Three Gaps Remain — All Closed in L8
1
Imprecise exceptions
Results reach registers out of order; 
at an exception “earlier done, later 
undone” cannot be guaranteed
Interrupts, page faults and traps 
require an ordered visible state
→ L8: reorder buffer (ROB) + 
in-order commit; speculative results 
can then be squashed together
2
The window stops at 
branches
Until the direction is known the 
window is confined to 
4–7-instruction blocks
Branches are frequent; without 
crossing them a large window stays 
empty
→ L8: branch prediction + 
speculative execution; execute the 
predicted path, roll back through the 
ROB on a miss
3
Store→load RAW through 
memory
Whether addresses coincide is 
unknown until computed; a load 
cannot pass a store
Pointers make aliasing undecidable 
at compile time (the run-time 
counterpart of L6 GCD / restrict)
→ L8: memory disambiguation; 
loads speculatively pass stores, 
addresses checked afterward, 
violations replayed
With all three closed, classic Tomasulo becomes the modern speculative out-of-order core; L8 
then asks how much ILP this actually mines — the answer is the ILP wall and the turn toward 
DLP/TLP.
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 20. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

slides.title: Summary: Ready Instructions Go First
slides.text:
Summary: Ready Instructions Go First
1 · Motivation: head-of-line blocking
Ready independent instructions are held behind an unready head
2 · Scoreboarding (1964): central tables, out-of-order execution
No renaming → WAR/WAW still stall
3 · Tomasulo (1967): three mechanisms
Stations wait distributed (value or tag) · renaming at issue removes WAR/WAW · the CDB broadcast wakes every waiter and 
forwards in the same step
4 · Three phases
Issue (rename into a station; structural hazards block here) → execute (wait for RAW tags; out of order) → write result 
(broadcast, free; out-of-order completion)
5 · Window value: fill waits with independent work; with non-blocking caches, MLP
RAW chains such as pointer chasing cannot be filled
In one sentence: dynamic ILP uses tags at run time to track the real data flow, letting 
operand-ready instructions pass unready ones while preserving RAW order exactly. L6 posed 
the problem, L7 built the engine, and L8 adds commit and speculation before reaching the ILP wall.
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 21. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

slides.text:
Further Reading & Tools

Approach (6e) — §3.4 (the CDC 6600 scoreboard), §3.5 (Tomasulo:

timing example), §3.6 (ROB and speculation; detailed in L8)

slides.title: Appendix: Glossary (1/2)
slides.text:
Appendix: Glossary (1/2)
Issue (enter an RS/buffer and rename) → [wait for operands as “value or tag”] → Execute → Write result (CDB 
broadcast)   [+ in-order Commit / ROB — L8]
Term Definition Notes / examples
Dynamic scheduling Hardware decides cycle by cycle at run time when each instruction uses which 
functional unit; timing decisions are not fixed in machine code.
Counterpart to L6 compiler scheduling; scoreboarding and 
Tomasulo are both dynamic.
Head-of-line blocking When the head of an ordered queue cannot be served, ready elements behind 
it cannot be served either.
Slide 4: a missing load and a RAW fadd block an 
independent fadd; out-of-order issue removes it.
Scoreboard
The CDC 6600’s centralized dynamic scheduler: three tables (instruction status, 
unit status, register result status) answer whether to issue, read operands, or 
write results.
In-order issue, out-of-order execution and write result; no 
renaming — WAR stalls at write result, WAW at issue.
Architectural / physical 
register
Architectural registers are ISA-defined and named in encodings (f2, x1); 
physical registers are the actual result-holding cells, more numerous.
A tag is a physical result location temporarily provided by a 
station; in modern cores it is a physical register number.
Tag / Qi / V, Q fields
A tag is the unique hardware name of an in-flight instruction’s result; Qi[f] 
names the station that will currently write register f; V holds a known operand 
value, Q the tag of its producer.
An empty Q means the operand is ready; slide 14: I2 has 
Qj=L1.
Reservation station / issue 
queue
A small hardware queue in front of a functional unit holding 
issued-but-not-started instructions; each entry holds Op, Vj/Vk, Qj/Qk, busy 
(memory buffers also A).
Classic term: reservation station; modern cores say issue 
queue or scheduler, same role.
Hardware register renaming At issue, architectural names map to tag-named physical result locations, so 
every in-flight writer has a unique name.
Removes WAR/WAW; cannot remove RAW (kept as a tag 
chain).
Common data bus (CDB) The shared bus broadcasting (producer tag, value) from a functional unit to all 
stations, memory buffers and the register file simultaneously.
Typically one result per cycle with arbitration; the 
generalization of L3 forwarding.
Wakeup / select
Two combinational steps per cycle: compare the broadcast tag against all Q 
fields in parallel (wakeup); arbitration picks among ready entries with free 
units (select).
Must complete in one clock cycle; dedicated 
comparator/arbitration circuits, not software.
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 23. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

slides.title: Appendix: Glossary (2/2)
slides.text:
Appendix: Glossary (2/2)
Term Definition Notes / examples
Issue / dispatch 
(terminology note)
In the classic paper “issue” means entering a station and renaming 
(used here); in modern pipelines this is usually “dispatch”, while 
“issue” means leaving the queue for a unit once operands are ready.
gem5/O3CPU documentation uses the modern 
usage; this lecture’s board work follows the classic 
three-phase wording.
In-/out-of-order issue, 
execution, completion
Issue, execution and completion (write result) may each follow 
program order or not; classic Tomasulo: issue in order, execution and 
completion out of order.
In the slide-14 walkthrough I3 executes and writes 
before I2.
Write result / writeback 
vs commit (retirement)
Write result: the result reaches waiters over the CDB and enters its 
(tag/physical) location, possibly out of order; commit: results become 
irrevocable architectural state in program order.
Classic Tomasulo has no commit step and writes 
registers directly (imprecise exceptions); commit is 
added by the L8 ROB.
Precise exception A machine state at exception time in which all instructions before the 
faulting one have completed and taken effect, and none after it has.
Out-of-order architectural writes break it; in-order 
commit with a ROB restores it (L8).
Out-of-order / instruction 
window
At any instant, the set of issued-but-incomplete instructions among 
which hardware freely selects ready ones to execute.
In the classic model, occupied station and buffer 
entries; in modern cores, roughly the ROB capacity.
MLP (memory-level 
parallelism)
Multiple independent cache misses in flight at once; requires a 
non-blocking cache with MSHRs (L5) and a window that keeps 
independent loads in flight.
Pointer chasing is a RAW chain with one miss in 
flight; Lab 8 Task 8.0 models L=10.
μop (micro-op) A RISC-like internal operation decoded from a CISC instruction (e.g. 
x86); Tomasulo-style scheduling works in μops.
The Pentium Pro (1995) fusion: μops + Tomasulo + 
ROB; defined also in the L6 glossary.
slides.notes: Source: lecture7-preview.pdf, page 24. Original lecture by Huan Wang, Westlake University, Fall 2026.

lectures.title: How computers execute programs
lectures.summary: CPU execution, memory locality, and the limits of parallel speedup.

slides.title: From program to processor
slides.lead: A program becomes a sequence of machine instructions.
bullets: The compiler translates source code into instructions.
The processor reads instructions and operands, computes, and stores results.
Goal: connect program structure with execution cost.

slides.title: The instruction cycle
slides.lead: Fetch → decode → execute → write back.
bullets: The program counter identifies the next instruction.
Registers hold values close to the execution units.
Real processors overlap work; this cycle is a conceptual model.
slides.notes: A modern CPU may decode multiple instructions per cycle and execute out of order. Do not treat the simple cycle as a hardware timing guarantee.

slides.title: Measure execution time
slides.lead: A faster clock alone does not guarantee a faster program.
bullets: Instruction count depends on the program, compiler, and instruction set.
CPI means average cycles per instruction for this workload.
Example: 1 billion instructions × 2 CPI / 2 GHz = 1 second.

slides.title: Why caches matter
slides.lead: Repeated access to nearby data can reduce memory stalls.
bullets: Temporal locality: reuse a recently accessed value.
Spatial locality: access values stored close together.
A row-wise traversal often suits a row-major array.
slides.notes: Use a sufficiently wide total and valid array bounds. Cache behavior depends on layout, dimensions, and hardware.

slides.title: Parallel work has a serial part
slides.lead: Only the parallel portion benefits from extra workers.
bullets: Let p be the parallel fraction and N the number of workers.
If p = 0.9 and N = 4, ideal speedup is about 3.08.
Communication and scheduling can reduce real speedup.
slides.notes: Amdahl’s law here assumes a fixed problem size, no extra overhead, and perfectly scalable parallel work.

slides.title: Shared data needs coordination
slides.lead: Two threads updating one value can lose an update.
bullets: Read-modify-write is not automatically atomic.
Use a reduction, atomic operation, or appropriate synchronization.
Choose independent work before adding more threads.

slides.title: Check your understanding
slides.lead: A workload is 80% parallel. What is its ideal speedup on 4 workers?
bullets: Explain why the speedup is less than 4.
Name one cache-friendly change to a numerical loop.
Compare the assumptions with a real application.
slides.notes: Answer: 1/(0.2+0.8/4)=2.5. The serial portion limits speedup; real overhead may reduce it further.

lectures.title: Decomposing work for parallel execution
lectures.summary: Data parallelism, task parallelism, and safe reductions.

slides.title: Find independent work
slides.lead: Parallel execution starts with identifying work that can overlap.
bullets: A dependency requires one result before another step can begin.
Independent operations may run concurrently.
Goal: design a decomposition before choosing a thread count.

slides.title: Data parallelism
slides.lead: Apply the same operation to independent pieces of data.
bullets: Scale every pixel in an image.
Add corresponding elements of two arrays.
Split the index range into chunks; avoid overlapping writes.
slides.notes: Illustrative sequential C++; parallel execution needs an explicit runtime. Assume equally sized arrays and no overlapping input/output storage.

slides.title: Task parallelism
slides.lead: Run different tasks when their inputs are ready.
bullets: Load one independent resource while processing another.
A dependency graph records which tasks must wait.
The longest dependency chain limits completion time.

slides.title: Reductions combine local results
slides.lead: Give each worker a private accumulator, then combine them.
bullets: Partition the input without overlap.
Compute one partial sum per worker.
Combine partial sums after those workers finish.
slides.notes: Chunks C_j form a partition. Floating-point addition is not associative; changing the order may change rounding. Integer accumulation can overflow.

slides.title: Balance work and overhead
slides.lead: Small tasks increase scheduling cost; large tasks can leave workers idle.
bullets: Static chunks suit workloads with predictable cost.
Dynamic scheduling can help when task costs vary.
Measure the complete workload, including synchronization and transfers.

slides.title: Avoid false sharing
slides.lead: Independent variables can still share a cache line.
bullets: Different workers may repeatedly modify nearby values.
Cache coherence can move the shared cache line between cores.
Use private accumulation and combine results later when appropriate.
slides.notes: False sharing is a performance effect, not by itself a data race. Padding choices depend on actual hardware and layout.

slides.title: Check your understanding
slides.lead: How would you sum ten million values using four workers?
bullets: Describe the partition and ownership of each accumulator.
Identify the final synchronization point.
Explain why four workers need not produce a fourfold speedup.
slides.notes: Use disjoint chunks, private partial sums, then synchronize and combine. Memory bandwidth, scheduling, the serial combine, and rounding behavior all matter.

title: Linear Algebra
description: Vectors, transformations, and the geometry behind matrices.

lectures.title: Vectors and linear transformations
lectures.summary: Build intuition for combinations, independence, and matrix maps.

slides.title: Vectors describe direction and magnitude
slides.lead: Coordinates describe a vector relative to a chosen basis.
bullets: In the plane, (2, 1) means two units along the first basis vector and one along the second.
Changing coordinates does not necessarily change the geometric vector.
Goal: read a matrix as a transformation.

slides.title: Build a linear combination
slides.lead: Scale vectors, then add them.
bullets: The span is the set of all combinations of the chosen vectors.
Two nonparallel vectors span the plane.
Multiples of one nonzero vector span a line.

slides.title: A matrix is determined by its columns
slides.lead: The columns tell us where the standard basis vectors go.
bullets: The first column is the image of e₁.
The second column is the image of e₂.
Multiplication combines those columns using the input coordinates.

slides.title: What makes a map linear?
slides.lead: It preserves vector addition and scalar multiplication.
bullets: Scaling, rotations about the origin, and projections are linear.
A nonzero translation is not linear: it moves the origin.
Checking only T(0)=0 is necessary but not sufficient.

slides.title: Independence means no redundancy
slides.lead: Neither vector can be built from the other.
bullets: The vectors (1, 0) and (0, 1) are independent.
The vectors (1, 2) and (2, 4) are dependent.
A basis is an independent set that spans the space.

slides.title: A projection can lose information
slides.lead: Projection onto the x-axis keeps x and removes y.
bullets: The image is the x-axis.
Every vector on the y-axis maps to zero.
The map cannot be inverted because many inputs share one output.

slides.title: Check your understanding
bullets: Explain the answer as a combination of the columns.
Can the projection P be undone for every input? Why?
Next: eigenvectors identify directions a transformation preserves.
slides.notes: Answer: A(3,2)=(8,2). Projection cannot be undone globally because the original y-coordinate is lost.

title: Calculus
description: Understand change through limits, derivatives, and accumulation.

lectures.title: The derivative as a rate of change
lectures.summary: From secant slopes to tangent lines and local approximation.

slides.title: How fast is a quantity changing?
slides.lead: The derivative measures an instantaneous rate of change.
bullets: A position function gives location as a function of time.
Average velocity compares two different times.
Instantaneous velocity is the limit of those average rates.

slides.title: Start with an average rate
slides.lead: A secant line joins two points on a graph.
bullets: The numerator is the change in the output.
The denominator is the change in the input.
For f(x)=x², between x=2 and x=3 the slope is 5.

slides.title: Let the interval shrink
slides.lead: The derivative exists when the difference quotient approaches a finite limit.
bullets: The limit must agree from both sides for an interior point.
We take a limit; we do not substitute h=0 into a quotient.
A corner can prevent the derivative from existing.

slides.title: Differentiate x squared
slides.lead: Expand first, cancel, and then take the limit.
bullets: The difference quotient simplifies to 2a+h.
As h approaches zero, the slope approaches 2a.
At a=2, the tangent slope is 4.

slides.title: A tangent line is a local model
slides.lead: Near a, a differentiable function is approximately linear.
bullets: The tangent model predicts f(2.1) ≈ 4.4.
The actual value is 4.41; approximation quality depends on distance and curvature.

slides.title: Not every continuous curve has a tangent slope
slides.lead: The absolute-value function has a corner at zero.
bullets: From the left, the difference quotient is −1.
From the right, it is +1.
The function is continuous at zero, but it is not differentiable there.

slides.title: Check your understanding
slides.lead: Find the slope of x² at x=3 and its tangent-line estimate at x=3.02.
bullets: Write the derivative as a limit before using the result.
State the units if x is time and f(x) is position.
Explain why a continuous function may fail to be differentiable.
slides.notes: Slope: 6. Tangent estimate: 9+6(0.02)=9.12; exact value 9.1204. For position/time, the derivative has units of velocity.

lectures.title: Accumulation and the definite integral
lectures.summary: Riemann sums, signed area, and the Fundamental Theorem.

slides.title: From rate to total change
slides.lead: Integrals describe accumulation over an interval.
bullets: A rate gives change per unit of input.
Multiply the rate by a small interval to approximate a small change.
Add those changes across the interval.

slides.title: Build a Riemann sum
slides.lead: Partition the interval and sum rectangular contributions.
bullets: Each width is Δxᵢ.
Choose a sample point xᵢ* inside each subinterval.
The rectangle height is f(xᵢ*).

slides.title: Refine the partition
slides.lead: For a continuous function, the sums approach the definite integral.
bullets: The largest subinterval width must approach zero.
Different sample points give the same limit.
A definite integral is a number for fixed endpoints.

slides.title: Accumulation is signed
slides.lead: Contributions below the horizontal axis are negative.
bullets: The integral of an odd function over a symmetric interval is zero when it is integrable.
Zero signed area does not mean no region exists.
Use the integral of |f| when total geometric area is required.

slides.title: Connect accumulation and differentiation
slides.lead: An antiderivative lets us compute the integral from endpoint values.
bullets: Assume f is continuous on [a,b] and F′=f there.
Evaluate F at the upper endpoint and subtract its value at the lower endpoint.
The added constant in F cancels.

slides.title: Work a complete example
slides.lead: Accumulate the rate f(x)=2x from x=0 to x=3.
bullets: An antiderivative is F(x)=x².
The result is 3²−0²=9.
The triangle under the graph has base 3 and height 6, so its area is also 9.

slides.title: Check your understanding
slides.lead: Evaluate the integral of 3x² from 0 to 2.
bullets: Name an antiderivative before substituting endpoints.
Explain how rate units change after integration.
Distinguish net displacement from total distance.
slides.notes: Answer: [x³] from 0 to 2 = 8. Integrating velocity over time gives displacement; integrating the absolute value of velocity gives distance.

title: Data Structure and Algorithm Design
description: Choose representations, reason about cost, and design correct algorithms.

lectures.title: Hash functions · Interactive lab
lectures.summary: Original 10-slide introduction with guided hash visualizations and optional local C++ experiments.

slides.title: Hash functions: from a key to a bucket
slides.lead: A hash table separates hashing from storage.
bullets: A hash function maps a key to a fixed-size value.
A bucket index can be computed as hash(key) modulo the bucket count.
Open Visualize to experiment; Try C++ runs the same examples locally.
slides.notes: Original teaching example for the interactive hash lab. Demonstration algorithms are noncryptographic.

slides.title: Equality is the first contract
slides.lead: Equal keys must have equal hashes.
bullets: Fractions 1/2 and 2/4 represent the same value.
Normalize numerator and denominator before hashing.
Keep the denominator positive; reject zero denominators.
slides.notes: Original teaching example for the interactive hash lab. Demonstration algorithms are noncryptographic.

slides.title: Canonical forms
slides.lead: Choose one representation for each equal value.
bullets: Divide both parts of a fraction by their greatest common divisor.
Normalize the sign after reduction.
Different values may still produce the same hash.
slides.notes: Original teaching example for the interactive hash lab. Demonstration algorithms are noncryptographic.

slides.title: A simple string hash
slides.lead: Summing bytes is easy, but ignores their order.
bullets: Use UTF-8 bytes so the encoding is explicit.
The strings form and from have the same byte sum: 436.
This collision shows why order matters.
slides.notes: Original teaching example for the interactive hash lab. Demonstration algorithms are noncryptographic.

slides.title: Collisions are unavoidable
slides.lead: A finite hash space cannot uniquely represent unlimited keys.
bullets: A collision is different keys producing the same hash.
The table must compare keys when resolving a collision.
A demonstration hash is not a cryptographic guarantee.
slides.notes: Original teaching example for the interactive hash lab. Demonstration algorithms are noncryptographic.

slides.title: Horner-style hashing
slides.lead: Update a running hash as each byte arrives.
bullets: Start at zero.
For each UTF-8 byte b, compute h = 12347h + b modulo 2³².
Open the byte-by-byte example to inspect every update.
slides.notes: Original teaching example for the interactive hash lab. Demonstration algorithms are noncryptographic.

slides.title: Unsigned arithmetic
slides.lead: Make wraparound part of the algorithm.
bullets: The JavaScript model and C++ examples both use 32-bit unsigned values.
Multiplication and addition wrap modulo 2³².
Use std::uint32_t instead of relying on signed overflow.
slides.notes: Original teaching example for the interactive hash lab. Demonstration algorithms are noncryptographic.

slides.title: Sampling bytes
slides.lead: Reading fewer bytes trades away information.
bullets: Try positions 0, 1, 3, 7 and so on.
Changing a skipped byte cannot change this sampled hash.
Compare the result with hashing every byte.
slides.notes: Original teaching example for the interactive hash lab. Demonstration algorithms are noncryptographic.

slides.title: Bucket count and load factor
slides.lead: Distribution and table policy both affect performance.
bullets: Load factor α is the number of keys divided by the number of buckets.
Resizing controls load, but cannot fix a hash that sends every key to one bucket.
Expected constant-time lookup relies on assumptions about distribution.
slides.notes: Original teaching example for the interactive hash lab. Demonstration algorithms are noncryptographic.

slides.title: Test your explanation
slides.lead: Use the lab to challenge a claim.
bullets: Construct a collision for byte-sum hashing.
Explain why equal fractions need normalization.
Edit the C++ example, inspect the output, and share your reasoning in Discussions.
slides.notes: Original teaching example for the interactive hash lab. Demonstration algorithms are noncryptographic.

lectures.title: Searching, data structures, and complexity
lectures.summary: Compare linear and binary search using invariants and growth rates.

slides.title: The representation shapes the algorithm
slides.lead: Choose a data structure to support the operations you need.
bullets: An array supports direct access by index.
A linked list supports traversal through links.
The best choice depends on the workload, not a universal ranking.

slides.title: Start with linear search
slides.lead: Check elements one at a time until you find a match.
bullets: Works on unsorted input.
Worst case: inspect all n elements.
Best case: the first element matches.
slides.notes: Illustrative C++ snippet; include <vector> and <cstddef>. Assumes the size fits in int. This site displays code; it does not execute it.

slides.title: Binary search needs ordered input
slides.lead: Use the middle element to discard half of the remaining candidates.
bullets: Assume ascending order and efficient random access.
If the middle value is too small, keep only larger indices.
Sorting first has its own cost; count it when comparing one-off searches.

slides.title: Keep a precise search interval
slides.lead: Use the half-open interval [lo, hi).
bullets: Initially, every possible match is in [0, n).
If a[mid] is too small, set lo = mid+1.
Otherwise set hi = mid; this variant finds the first value not less than target.
slides.notes: Illustrative C++ fragment. a is an ascending std::vector<int>. Short-circuit evaluation makes the final access safe even when lo equals a.size(). Empty input is valid.

slides.title: Reason about growth
slides.lead: Binary search repeatedly halves the candidate interval.
bullets: Linear search has O(n) worst-case comparisons.
Binary search has O(log n) worst-case comparisons on an ordered array.
Big-O describes a growth bound, not exact elapsed time.

slides.title: Trace an example
slides.lead: Search for 7 in [1, 3, 5, 7, 9].
bullets: Start [0, 5): mid=2, value=5 → lo=3.
Next [3, 5): mid=4, value=9 → hi=4.
Next [3, 4): mid=3, value=7 → hi=3. Finish at index 3.

slides.title: Check your understanding
slides.lead: What happens when the target is absent or the array is empty?
bullets: Trace the interval for target 6 in [1, 3, 5, 7, 9].
Explain why a linked list does not offer the same random-access cost.
State the sorted-input assumption before choosing binary search.
slides.notes: Target 6: lower-bound index 3, found=false. Empty input: lo=hi=0 and found=false, with no element access. A linked list requires traversal to reach a middle element.

lectures.title: Stacks, queues, and graph traversal
lectures.summary: Use access order to design useful algorithms.

slides.title: Choose the next item deliberately
slides.lead: A data structure can encode the order in which work is processed.
bullets: A stack selects the most recently added item.
A queue selects the earliest added item.
Changing this order changes how a search explores a graph.

slides.title: A stack is last in, first out
slides.lead: Push adds an item; pop removes the most recently added item.
bullets: A stack can model nested function calls.
Balanced-parentheses checking needs to remember the latest unmatched opening symbol.
Check for emptiness before reading or removing the top.

slides.title: A queue is first in, first out
slides.lead: Enqueue at the back and dequeue from the front.
bullets: A queue models work arriving in order.
A deque or ring buffer can support efficient queue operations.
Repeatedly removing the first element of a contiguous array may require shifting.

slides.title: Depth-first search uses a stack
slides.lead: Explore a branch before returning to alternatives.
bullets: Keep a visited set when the graph can contain cycles.
An explicit stack can replace recursive calls.
DFS is useful for reachability and many dependency analyses.
slides.notes: A plain recursive DFS needs stack space proportional to recursion depth. Dependency ordering also requires detecting directed cycles.

slides.title: Breadth-first search uses a queue
slides.lead: Explore all vertices at one distance before the next distance.
bullets: Start with the source at distance zero.
Mark a vertex visited when it is enqueued.
In an unweighted graph, BFS finds shortest paths measured by edge count.
slides.notes: Illustrative C++ fragment. Assumes valid initialized graph and visited arrays, and a queue supporting these operations. Tracking actual distances or parents requires additional arrays.

slides.title: Account for vertices and edges
slides.lead: With adjacency lists, a complete traversal processes vertices and adjacency entries.
bullets: Standard BFS and DFS take O(V+E) time.
The visited structure and worklist use O(V) auxiliary space.
An adjacency matrix changes the neighbor-scanning cost.

slides.title: Check your understanding
slides.lead: Which structure finds shortest routes when every edge has equal cost?
bullets: Explain why processing vertices by distance matters.
Describe what can go wrong if visited is omitted in a cyclic graph.
Would the same shortest-path claim hold for arbitrary unequal edge weights?
slides.notes: Use BFS with a queue for equal-cost edges. Omitting visited can repeat work indefinitely. Arbitrary unequal weights require a suitable shortest-path algorithm; plain BFS is insufficient.
